blocks.body:
Almost every olympiad geometry solution, however clever, is assembled from a small stock of facts: the angles of a triangle add up to $180^\circ$, parallel lines create equal angles, similar triangles have proportional sides, and the laws of sines and cosines convert between angles and lengths. This lesson collects that stock with proofs, so that you know not only the facts but also exactly when they apply.

Notation used throughout: in triangle $ABC$ the side lengths are $a = BC$, $b = CA$, $c = AB$; the angles at $A, B, C$ are also called $A, B, C$; $R$ is the radius of the circumcircle (the circle through $A$, $B$, $C$); and $[ABC]$ denotes the area.

blocks.title: Angles and parallel lines
blocks.body:
When two lines cross, opposite (vertical) angles are equal. When a line crosses two parallel lines, it makes equal angles with them in matching positions: corresponding angles are equal and alternate angles are equal. Conversely, equal alternate angles force the two lines to be parallel. The statement that parallel lines produce equal alternate angles is where Euclid's parallel postulate is used.

The angle sum of a triangle follows at once. Draw the line through $A$ parallel to $BC$. The two angles it makes with $AB$ and $AC$ are alternate to the angles $B$ and $C$, and together with the angle $A$ they fill a straight angle. So
$$A + B + C = 180^\circ.$$
Two consequences are used constantly. The exterior angle at a vertex equals the sum of the two interior angles at the other vertices, since both equal $180^\circ$ minus the interior angle at that vertex. And a convex $n$-gon has angle sum $(n-2)\cdot 180^\circ$, as one sees by cutting it into $n - 2$ triangles from one vertex.

Angle chasing means: name a few unknown angles, express every other angle in terms of them using these rules, and read off the relation you want. The other basic source of equal angles is the isosceles triangle: if $AB = AC$ then $B = C$, and conversely.

blocks.title: An angle chase
blocks.body: The bisectors of angles $B$ and $C$ of triangle $ABC$ meet at $I$. Express $\angle BIC$ in terms of $A$.
blocks.solution:
In triangle $IBC$ the angles at $B$ and $C$ are $B/2$ and $C/2$. So
$$\angle BIC = 180^\circ - \frac{B + C}{2} = 180^\circ - \frac{180^\circ - A}{2} = 90^\circ + \frac A2.$$
For example, if $A = 60^\circ$ then $\angle BIC = 120^\circ$, whatever $B$ and $C$ are. The point $I$ is the incentre.

blocks.title: Congruence and similarity
blocks.body:
Two triangles are congruent if one can be moved onto the other by a rigid motion, so that all corresponding sides and angles agree. Three pieces of data suffice, in the right combinations:

- SSS: three pairs of equal sides.
- SAS: two pairs of equal sides and equal angles between them.
- ASA or AAS: one pair of equal sides and two pairs of equal angles (by the angle sum, the third angles then agree too).
- RHS: right triangles with equal hypotenuses and one other pair of equal sides.

Two sides and an angle that is not between them (SSA) do not determine a triangle; see the pitfalls.

Two triangles are similar if their angles agree. Then their sides are proportional with a common ratio $k$, and their areas are in ratio $k^2$. The criteria are AA (two pairs of equal angles), SAS-similarity (two pairs of sides in the same ratio with equal angles between them) and SSS-similarity (all three pairs of sides in the same ratio). When writing $\triangle ABC \sim \triangle DEF$, list the vertices in corresponding order; then $AB/DE = BC/EF = CA/FD$ can be read off directly.

The engine behind similarity is the intercept theorem: if a line parallel to $BC$ meets $AB$ at $D$ and $AC$ at $E$, then $AD/AB = AE/AC$. Here is a proof with areas. Triangles $BDE$ and $CDE$ have the same base $DE$ and, since $DE \parallel BC$, the same height, so they have equal areas. Adding triangle $ADE$ to each gives $[ABE] = [ACD]$. Now triangles $ADE$ and $ABE$ share the vertex $E$ and have bases $AD$ and $AB$ on one line, so $[ADE]/[ABE] = AD/AB$. Likewise $[ADE]/[ACD] = AE/AC$. The two left-hand sides are equal, hence so are the right-hand sides.

blocks.title: Area
blocks.body:
The basic formula is $[ABC] = \frac12 a h_a$, where $h_a$ is the height from $A$ to line $BC$. Since $h_a = b\sin C$, from the right triangle formed by $A$, $C$ and the foot of the height (also when $C$ is obtuse, because $\sin(180^\circ - C) = \sin C$), we get
$$[ABC] = \tfrac12 ab\sin C = \tfrac12 bc\sin A = \tfrac12 ca\sin B.$$
Heron's formula gives the area from the sides alone: with $s = \frac{a+b+c}2$,
$$[ABC] = \sqrt{s(s-a)(s-b)(s-c)}.$$
It can be derived by combining $\frac12 ab\sin C$ with the law of cosines below.

The most useful area fact in competitions is also the simplest: triangles with the same height have areas proportional to their bases. For $D$ on segment $BC$ it gives $\dfrac{BD}{DC} = \dfrac{[ABD]}{[ADC]}$, which converts length ratios into area ratios and back.

blocks.title: The angle bisector theorem
blocks.body: Prove the angle bisector theorem: if the bisector of angle $A$ meets $BC$ at $D$, then $BD/DC = AB/AC$. Then find $BD$ and $DC$ when $AB = 6$, $AC = 4$, $BC = 5$.
blocks.solution:
Compute the ratio $[ABD]/[ADC]$ in two ways. Both triangles have the same height from $A$, so the ratio is $BD/DC$. Also, using the formula $\frac12 xy\sin\theta$ with the two sides at $A$,
$$\frac{[ABD]}{[ADC]} = \frac{\frac12\, AB\cdot AD\sin\frac A2}{\frac12\, AC\cdot AD\sin\frac A2} = \frac{AB}{AC}.$$
Hence $BD/DC = AB/AC$.

With the given numbers, $BD/DC = 6/4 = 3/2$ and $BD + DC = 5$, so $BD = 3$ and $DC = 2$.

blocks.title: Central angle theorem
blocks.body: Let $A$, $B$, $C$ be points on a circle with centre $O$. Then $\angle BAC$ is half of the central angle that stands on the arc $BC$ not containing $A$. (This central angle exceeds $180^\circ$ when $\angle BAC$ is obtuse.)

Let $A'$ be the point of the circle diametrically opposite $A$. Triangle $OAB$ is isosceles with $OA = OB$, so its angles at $A$ and $B$ are equal, and the exterior angle at $O$ is their sum: $\angle BOA' = 2\angle BAA'$. In the same way $\angle COA' = 2\angle CAA'$.

If the diameter $AA'$ lies inside the angle $BAC$, then $\angle BAC = \angle BAA' + \angle A'AC$, and the arc $BC$ not containing $A$ is made up of the arcs $BA'$ and $A'C$, so its central angle is $\angle BOA' + \angle A'OC = 2\angle BAC$. If $AA'$ lies outside the angle, say with ray $AB$ between rays $AA'$ and $AC$, then $\angle BAC = \angle A'AC - \angle A'AB$ and the arc $BC$ is the arc $A'C$ minus the arc $A'B$, so again the central angle is $2\angle BAC$. If $A'$ coincides with $B$ or $C$, one of the two pieces is zero and the same computation works.

Two consequences are used everywhere: angles standing on the same arc from the same side are equal, and an angle standing on a diameter is a right angle (Thales). The lesson [[circles]] develops these further.

blocks.title: Law of sines
blocks.body:
In every triangle,
$$\frac{a}{\sin A} = \frac{b}{\sin B} = \frac{c}{\sin C} = 2R.$$

blocks.title: Law of cosines
blocks.body: In every triangle $c^2 = a^2 + b^2 - 2ab\cos C$, and similarly for the other two sides.

Place $C$ at the origin and $B$ at $(a, 0)$. The point $A$ is at distance $b$ from $C$ in the direction making the angle $C$ with the positive $x$-axis, so $A = (b\cos C, b\sin C)$; this description is valid whether $C$ is acute, right or obtuse. Hence
$$c^2 = AB^2 = (a - b\cos C)^2 + (b\sin C)^2 = a^2 - 2ab\cos C + b^2(\cos^2 C + \sin^2 C) = a^2 + b^2 - 2ab\cos C.$$
For $C = 90^\circ$ this is Pythagoras' theorem. In general the sign of $a^2 + b^2 - c^2$ tells whether $C$ is acute, right or obtuse.

blocks.title: Solving a triangle
blocks.body: A triangle has sides $a = 7$, $b = 5$, $c = 3$. Find the angle $A$, the circumradius $R$ and the area, and check the area with Heron's formula.
blocks.solution:
By the law of cosines,
$$\cos A = \frac{b^2 + c^2 - a^2}{2bc} = \frac{25 + 9 - 49}{30} = -\frac12,$$
so $A = 120^\circ$. By the law of sines, $R = \dfrac{a}{2\sin A} = \dfrac{7}{2\cdot\frac{\sqrt3}{2}} = \dfrac{7}{\sqrt3} = \dfrac{7\sqrt3}{3}$. The area is $\frac12 bc\sin A = \frac12\cdot 5\cdot 3\cdot\frac{\sqrt3}2 = \frac{15\sqrt3}{4}$.

Heron: $s = \frac{15}{2}$, and $s - a = \frac12$, $s - b = \frac52$, $s - c = \frac92$, so
$$s(s-a)(s-b)(s-c) = \frac{15\cdot 1\cdot 5\cdot 9}{16} = \frac{675}{16}, \qquad \sqrt{\frac{675}{16}} = \frac{15\sqrt3}{4},$$
in agreement. A third route: substituting $\sin C = c/(2R)$ into $\frac12 ab\sin C$ gives $[ABC] = \dfrac{abc}{4R}$, here $\dfrac{105}{4}\cdot\dfrac{\sqrt3}{7} = \dfrac{15\sqrt3}{4}$.

blocks.title: Perpendicular medians
blocks.body: In triangle $ABC$ the medians from $A$ and from $B$ are perpendicular. Prove that $a^2 + b^2 = 5c^2$.
blocks.solution:
Step 1: the length of a median. Let $M$ be the midpoint of $BC$ and $m_a = AM$. Apply the law of cosines in triangles $AMB$ and $AMC$, which share the side $AM$ and have $BM = MC = a/2$:
$$c^2 = m_a^2 + \tfrac{a^2}{4} - a\,m_a\cos\angle AMB, \qquad b^2 = m_a^2 + \tfrac{a^2}4 - a\,m_a\cos\angle AMC.$$
Since $\angle AMB + \angle AMC = 180^\circ$, the two cosines are negatives of each other, and adding gives $b^2 + c^2 = 2m_a^2 + \frac{a^2}2$. So
$$m_a^2 = \frac{2b^2 + 2c^2 - a^2}{4}, \qquad\text{and likewise}\qquad m_b^2 = \frac{2a^2 + 2c^2 - b^2}{4}.$$

Step 2: the medians cut each other in ratio $2:1$. Let the medians $AM$ and $BN$ meet at $G$, where $N$ is the midpoint of $CA$. By SAS-similarity ($CM/CB = CN/CA = \frac12$ with the common angle $C$), triangle $CMN$ is similar to $CBA$, so $MN \parallel AB$ and $MN = \frac12 AB$. Then triangles $GAB$ and $GMN$ have equal angles (alternate angles at the parallel lines), so they are similar with ratio $2$, and $AG = 2\,GM$, $BG = 2\,GN$. Hence $AG = \frac23 m_a$ and $BG = \frac23 m_b$.

Step 3: Pythagoras in the right triangle $AGB$:
$$c^2 = AG^2 + BG^2 = \frac49\left(m_a^2 + m_b^2\right) = \frac49\cdot\frac{a^2 + b^2 + 4c^2}{4} = \frac{a^2 + b^2 + 4c^2}{9}.$$
So $9c^2 = a^2 + b^2 + 4c^2$, that is, $a^2 + b^2 = 5c^2$. Read backwards, using the converse of Pythagoras' theorem, the computation also shows that $a^2 + b^2 = 5c^2$ forces the two medians to be perpendicular.

blocks.title: Euclid and the parallel postulate
blocks.body:
Euclid's Elements, written around 300 BC, derived the geometry of its time from a short list of postulates and served as the model of a rigorous theory for two thousand years. (Its Book IX also proves that there are infinitely many primes; see [[fta]].) The fifth postulate, about parallel lines, looked less self-evident than the others, and for centuries mathematicians tried to derive it from them. Given the other axioms, it is equivalent to facts used above, such as the angle sum of every triangle being $180^\circ$, or the existence of two similar triangles that are not congruent.

In the nineteenth century Bolyai and Lobachevsky (and Gauss, privately) showed that a consistent geometry exists in which the parallel postulate fails. In this hyperbolic geometry the angle sum of a triangle is less than $180^\circ$ and similar triangles are congruent. So the facts in this lesson are facts about flat space, not consequences of logic alone.

- SSA is not a congruence test. With $A = 30^\circ$, $AC = 10$ and $BC = 6$ there are two different triangles: the distance from $C$ to the other side of the angle is $10\sin 30^\circ = 5$, and since $5 < 6 < 10$, the circle of radius $6$ about $C$ meets that side twice. The two possible values of $AB$ are $5\sqrt3 \pm \sqrt{11}$.
- The same ambiguity appears in the law of sines: $\sin A = \sin(180^\circ - A)$, so knowing $\sin A$ does not determine $A$.
- Similar triangles with ratio $k$ have areas in ratio $k^2$, not $k$.
- Reading angles off a diagram can fail in another configuration, such as an obtuse triangle or a point on the other side of a line. Check whether your argument depends on the picture.

[[circles]] develops inscribed angles, cyclic quadrilaterals and power of a point, and [[triangle-centres]] studies the incentre, circumcentre and their relatives. The sine and cosine used here are developed in [[trig]]. Coordinates, [[vectors-plane]] and complex numbers give algebraic routes to the same facts ([[analytic-geometry]]). Inequalities between $a$, $b$, $c$, $R$ and the area are the subject of [[geo-inequalities]], and configurations of many points and lines appear in [[discrete-geometry]].

1. In triangle $ABC$ with $AB = AC$ and $A = 36^\circ$, the bisector of angle $B$ meets $AC$ at $D$. Show that $BC = BD = AD$, and deduce that $BC/AB = \frac{\sqrt5 - 1}{2}$.
2. Prove that $a = b\cos C + c\cos B$ in every triangle.
3. A triangle has sides $13$, $14$, $15$. Find its area, its circumradius and the length of the median to the side of length $14$.
4. Prove that a triangle has a right angle if and only if $\sin^2 A + \sin^2 B + \sin^2 C = 2$.
